topics.name: Modals of deduction (must have / can't have)

options: I decided taking the grassy path.
I decided to take the grassy path.
I decided take the grassy path.
questions.rule: Decide is followed by the infinitive: decided to take.

options: Despite of the rain, we went for a walk in the woods.
Despite the rain, we went for a walk in the woods.
Despite it rained, we went for a walk in the woods.
questions.rule: Despite takes a noun directly (no of) and is not followed by a full clause.

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct verb forms.
options: If he would have taken the other road, he would have reached the river.
If he had taken the other road, he will have reached the river.
If he had taken the other road, he would have reached the river.
questions.rule: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

options: The ground is wet, so it must have rained last night.
The ground is wet, so it must rained last night.
The ground is wet, so it must has rained last night.
questions.rule: A sure guess about the past: must have + past participle.

options: Choose a career is not an easy task.
Choosing a career is not an easy task.
Chose a career is not an easy task.
questions.rule: An action used as the subject takes the gerund (-ing form): Choosing a career is ...

options: The first road looked fine; however, he has took the other one.
The first road looked fine; however, he taking the other one.
The first road looked fine; however, he took the other one.
questions.rule: After ; however, you need a full clause with a proper past verb: he took. 'Has took' and 'he taking' are wrong.

options: If Neha had practised more, she would have won the match.
If Neha had practised more, she would won the match.
If Neha had practise more, she would have won the match.
questions.rule: Past perfect needs the past participle (had practised); the result is would have won.

options: Arjun can't have chosen science; he hates physics.
Arjun can't have choose science; he hates physics.
Arjun can't has chosen science; he hates physics.
questions.rule: To say something is impossible in the past: can't have + past participle (chosen).

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: After a preposition like of, use the gerund: fond of reading.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Although needs a full clause. Before a noun phrase (her aching legs) use despite.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Third conditional result clause: would have + past participle.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Must have is followed by the past participle: must have walked.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A verb after the preposition of takes the -ing form: thinking of choosing.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: With would not have written, the if-clause needs the past perfect: had not stopped.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A full clause (he loves cricket) needs Although; Despite takes a noun or -ing form.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Can't have + past participle: can't have seen. Saw is the simple past, not the participle.
Want is followed by the infinitive: wanted to travel.

questions.after: the path was steep, we reached the top.
questions.rule: Although joins a contrasting clause. However cannot join two clauses with a comma; Despite needs a noun.

questions.before: If you had left earlier, you
questions.rule: Had left (past perfect) pairs with would have caught for an unreal past.

questions.before: The leaves are not crushed, so people
questions.rule: Uncrushed leaves show it is impossible: can't have used. After a modal always use have + past participle.
In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it takes the -ing form: meeting.

questions.after: his doubts, he took the less-travelled road.
questions.rule: His doubts is a noun phrase, not a clause, so use Despite.

questions.before: Riya would have won the race if she
questions.rule: With would have won, the if-clause takes the past perfect: had not fallen.

questions.before: If he had taken the other road, he
questions.rule: Past condition, present result (now): had taken ... would be.
Decide + infinitive: decided to walk.
Despite + noun phrase, then the main clause.

questions.prompt: Make a sentence that shows a sure guess about the past.
questions.rule: Must have been = I am sure it was.
Result would have helped + if + past perfect (had known).

questions.prompt: Make a sentence about a regret.
questions.rule: Regret + perfect gerund (not having chosen) talks about an earlier action.

chat: What do you enjoy doing on Sundays?
options: I enjoy cycling with my friends.
I enjoy to cycle with my friends.
I enjoy cycle with my friends.
questions.rule: Enjoy is followed by the gerund: enjoy cycling.

chat: Did you go to the park yesterday?
options: No. Because of the rain, we stayed in.
No. Although it rained, so we stayed in.
No. Because the rain, we stayed in.
questions.rule: Before a noun use because of. Although and so are never used together.

chat: Did you watch the final yesterday?
options: No. If I would have known it was on, I would have watched it.
No. If I had known it was on, I would have watched it.
No. If I had known it was on, I will watch it.
questions.rule: Unreal past: If I had known, I would have watched. Never put would have in the if-clause.

options: You must have leave them in the car.
You must have left them in the car.
You must had left them in the car.
questions.rule: A sure guess about the past: must have + past participle (left).

chat: Why did you stop at the shop on the way?
options: I stopped to buy some water.
I stopped for buy some water.
questions.rule: Stop to do gives the purpose of stopping: stopped to buy.

chat: Are you taking science or commerce?
options: Science. I love biology; moreover, I wants to be a doctor.
Science. I love biology; moreover, I want be a doctor.
Science. I love biology; moreover, I want to be a doctor.
questions.rule: With I, use want, and want takes the infinitive: want to be.

options: I had a fever. If I had been well, I would have come.
I had a fever. If I had been well, I would had come.
I had a fever. If I had been well, I will come.
questions.rule: Third conditional: If I had been ..., I would have come.

chat: Do you think he was angry?
options: He can't have be angry; he must have been asleep.
He can't have been angry; he must have been asleep.
He can't had been angry; he must have been asleep.
questions.rule: Past deduction: can't have been (impossible) and must have been (sure).

questions.prompt: Rewrite using a gerund as the subject.
questions.source: To walk in the woods is relaxing.
options: Walking in the woods is relaxing.
Walk in the woods is relaxing.
Walked in the woods is relaxing.
questions.rule: The infinitive subject To walk becomes the gerund Walking.

questions.source: The road was less travelled. He took it.
options: Although the road was less travelled, but he took it.
Although the road was less travelled, he took it.
Although the road was less travelled, he taken it.
questions.rule: Do not add but after an although clause; the simple past is took, not taken.

questions.source: He did not take the first road. He did not see the river.
options: If he had taken the first road, he would have seen the river.
If he took the first road, he would see the river.
If he had taken the first road, he would saw the river.
questions.rule: Facts in the past become a third conditional: If he had taken ..., he would have seen.

questions.source: I am sure that Aman forgot the meeting.
options: Aman must have forgot the meeting.
Aman must have forgotten the meeting.
questions.rule: Must have + past participle; the participle of forget is forgotten.

questions.source: Although she was afraid, Meera chose the dark path.
options: Despite she was afraid, Meera chose the dark path.
Despite being afraid, Meera chose the dark path.
Despite of being afraid, Meera chose the dark path.
questions.rule: Despite + -ing form (being afraid), with no of and no full clause.

questions.source: He did not take the busy road. He took the quiet one.
options: Instead of take the busy road, he took the quiet one.
Instead of to take the busy road, he took the quiet one.
Instead of taking the busy road, he took the quiet one.
questions.rule: Instead of is a preposition, so the verb after it takes -ing: taking.

questions.source: If I had known the way, I would have gone alone.
options: Had I know the way, I would have gone alone.
Had I known the way, I would have gone alone.
Had known I the way, I would have gone alone.
questions.rule: Drop if and put Had before the subject: Had I known.

questions.source: Both roads looked the same, but he chose the grassy one.
options: Both roads looked the same; however, he choose the grassy one.
Both roads looked the same; however, he chose the grassy one.
Both roads looked the same; however, he chosen the grassy one.
questions.rule: Use ; however, between the clauses and keep the simple past chose (not choose or chosen).

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this note.
questions.rule: Hope + infinitive: hopes to study. After the preposition at, use -ing: good at playing.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: Want + to + base verb: wanted to visit. Before a noun (the delay) use Despite.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: Had and would have need past participles: had listened, would have chosen, had thought.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: Deduction about the past: can't have walked, must have come. After a modal, always have, never has.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: Manage + infinitive: manages to finish. Enjoy + gerund: enjoys playing.
